1:
The book takes its name from its opening words; the name it goes by in English came from elsewhere. Keil and Delitzsch trace the Hebrew title to this first phrase, and the Greek and Latin one to a rabbinic description drawn from the law of the king — a repetition of the law — which the Septuagint and Vulgate turned into Deuteronomium. They think the rendering of that passage mistaken and the title still apt, since it does describe the leading contents; though on their reading the book is less a recapitulation of Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers than a compendium of the whole law and wisdom of the people. Clarke adds the rabbinic name meaning the iteration or doubling, and a fourth from nearer home: our Saxon ancestors called it the after law.

Who heard it is a fair question given the numbers. The whole body could not have been addressed at once without a miracle, so Gill understands the audience as the heads and representatives of the people, convened to hear and carry it back — unless we suppose Moses delivered the same things over again to one party after another. Henry pictures a great auditory all the same, with the elders and officers among them, and guesses it was a sabbath.

Where they stood matters to the argument. Henry notes that they were in the plain of Moab, on the edge of Canaan and of a war with the Canaanites — and that Moses says nothing about the arts and stratagems of war, only about their duty to God, on the principle that if they kept themselves in his favour their religion would be their best policy.

The geography of the opening verse is difficult, and the two who work at it disagree at several points. Clarke denies that the phrase rendered on this side Jordan settles any side at all — the word serves for either, and here means simply the ford where Israel would cross; he also denies that the Red Sea is named, since the word for sea is absent and the remaining word does not by itself mean that sea, and suspects a place, citing Ptolemy's Sophonites in Arabia Petraea. Ellicott takes the same word for the Gulf of Akabah, the Jewish paraphrasts having had no difficulty reading it so, and the plain looking straight down to that gulf. On the plain he is the more definite — the Arabah, here the valley running from the lower end of the Dead Sea to the head of the gulf — and he notes that the phrase about the wilderness cannot strictly govern what follows, that plain lying on neither side of Jordan.

The five names are read as two groups. Ellicott renders it as between Paran on one side and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth and Dizahab on the other, identifies two of them on the ground and supposes Laban to be some white place named from its rocks, and concludes that the verse traces the line of march from Sinai to Kadesh-barnea. Clarke observes that this Paran cannot be the one beside the Red Sea, being far from it. On the last name both reach for its meaning: Clarke separates it into two words and notes that the Septuagint made it gold mines, while Ellicott passes on the Jewish reading of it as gold enough and the guess that this was where the calf was burned and ground to dust and cast into the brook — a name earned by the apparent waste of precious metal, and by a people who had enough of that calf before they were done with it.

Then the second verse, which does nothing but state a distance, and Henry hears the reproach in it. Horeb was eleven days from Kadesh-barnea; the arithmetic is there to remind them that their own conduct had turned eleven days into forty years.
3:
The date is given to the day, and Keil and Delitzsch explain why it is worth giving. The first of the eleventh month in the fortieth year is near the end of a life and after the close of the divine lawgiving, so that Moses could speak according to all that the Lord had commanded him — the legislation already on record in the earlier books, which this book always refers to in that way. Wesley draws a double conclusion from the phrase: what follows is in substance what had been commanded before, and God now commanded him to repeat it, so that the rehearsal is itself by divine direction, a legacy left to the church.

Clarke reads the year as a season of bereavement: in its first month Miriam died, on the first day of the fifth Aaron, and about its close Moses himself. The book's whole span he measures exactly — from the first day of the eleventh month to the seventh of the twelfth, five weeks by lunar reckoning, with the history running a week past the death of Moses, then a hundred and twenty.

Ellicott hears a reproach in the opening word. The and is the real beginning of the book and ties it to the volumes before it; the moral of the date, he says, has been well pointed out by Jewish writers. Eleven days' journey lay between Sinai and the place from which the conquest should have started — but it was not eleven days of the second year that found Israel still short of it, but eleven months of the fortieth. They could not enter in because of unbelief.

The two victories named next are not decoration. Keil and Delitzsch make them part of the argument: by giving Israel Sihon and Og the Lord had begun to fulfil his promises, and had laid the people under an obligation of love and gratitude and obedience. Gill hesitates over the grammar, whether Moses speaks of himself in the third person or, as he prefers, ascribes the victory to the Lord.

What Moses then began to do is of some interest, because the verb is rare. Clarke glosses it as a willing undertaking, and the second as making bare — to explain fully. Ellicott takes the first as determined or assayed, and presses the second harder. It occurs in only two other places, and both connect it with writing: the words of the law written on stones very plainly, and the vision written plain upon tables. He concludes that Moses at this point began to throw the discourses and laws he had delivered into permanent form, from the motive Peter afterwards owned — that they might be able, after his decease, to have these things always in remembrance.

Calvin explains why a second exposition was needed. The Decalogue was brief, and brevity is obscurity to an ignorant and slow-hearted people, so God repeated the covenant with a fuller explanation attached; the word usually rendered beside adds nothing new but marks a repetition made in order to be understood. That he did this within sight of the land, forty years after the first promulgation, Calvin calls an extraordinary proof of indulgence — and notes the reason: he had now to do with a new generation.

Ellicott closes the introduction by dividing what the discourse will cover into three unequal periods. First the march from Sinai to Kadesh-barnea with the sending of the spies, whose characteristic is failure in leaders and people alike. Then thirty-seven and a half years of disgrace, marked in the record by the absence of any note of time or place — though it was also a period of training. Then the fortieth year, in which Sihon and Og fell and Israel reached the Jordan, the sentence on the older generation carried out and a new life begun.
6:
The first thing Moses recalls is a command to leave. Gill identifies Horeb with Sinai; Clarke measures the stay — they reached it in the third month after Egypt and left on the twentieth of the second month of the following year, so nearly a whole year had passed. Ellicott calls that interval the period of organisation, in which the people received the Law and were formed into a church militant, an army encamped round the tabernacle — a single year whose institutions fill a third of the Pentateuch.

Keil and Delitzsch read both halves of the sentence as loaded. The title Jehovah our God presupposes the reception of Israel into covenant, which happened at this mountain; and to say they had dwelt there long enough is to say the purpose of bringing them had been answered — they now had the laws and ordinances the covenant required, and could go and take the land. They add a candid note about the source: this word of the Lord is not found in this form in the earlier history, though it is contained in substance in the instructions that prepared the removal and in the lifting of the cloud.

Calvin insists that a sign was not thought sufficient. God lifted the cloud and also spoke, telling them in words that enough time had been spent in one place. And because eleven days' journey still lay between them and Kadesh, and the people were naturally indolent, the command is framed to make the thing look easy: they had only to lift up their feet and go, and the promised rest was theirs.

Henry takes the leaving as a mercy rather than a dismissal. This was the mount that burned with fire and gendered to bondage; God brought them there to humble them and to prepare them by the terrors of the law for the land of promise, kept them about a year, and then told them the year was enough. Though he brings his people into affliction of mind, he knows when they have dwelt long enough in it, and will find the fittest time to advance them.

What they were sent to is described by its parts, and the parts are disputed only in emphasis. Keil and Delitzsch take the mount of the Amorites for the hill-country that is the leading feature of Canaan, the Amorites standing for all the tribes as the most powerful of them, so that the phrase is equivalent to the land of the Canaanites. Ellicott is more specific, making it the southern part of Judah from which the five kings came up against Gibeon — the very territory Israel would have entered had they gone up from Kadesh by the way of the spies. Clarke reads the list as a boundary rather than a route, fixing the limits to which Israel's territory might extend if Canaan proper proved too small — south to the Amorite hills, west to the sea, north to Lebanon, east to the Euphrates — and observes that Solomon reigned to exactly that extent, so that in his day the promise to Abraham was fulfilled literally.

The grant is put in the perfect tense, and its force is taken seriously. Keil and Delitzsch note that the idiom means to place at a man's disposal, and that the swearing points back to the oath after the binding of Isaac; they are careful that to them and to their seed not be pressed into meaning the patriarchs should themselves have taken possession. Ellicott presses the opposite way — the land is promised to Abraham and to Isaac and to Jacob, not merely to their descendants, and the promise is not forgotten though all three are in another world. Wesley keeps to the plain sense: it is set before your faces, open to your view and your possession, and there is no impediment in the way.
9:
Moses turns from the march to the machinery of government, and dates the change loosely. Gill puts it after the rock at Horeb was smitten and before the encampment at Sinai, when Jethro gave the advice Moses acted on. Ellicott finds the passage a close expansion of that older counsel — that the judges must be able men who fear God, men of truth hating covetousness, a sentence he calls older than the Decalogue itself.

The complaint that opens it might be taken badly, and Keil and Delitzsch say the prayer is there to prevent that. Having said he could not bear them alone, Moses adds at once a wish that God would multiply the nation a thousandfold — and the blessing joined to the multiplying, they note, points back to the promise made to Abraham, so it is not merely strength and numbers that is meant but the spiritual blessing along with them. Gill reads the parenthesis the same way, as proof that he did not envy their increase or find it an uneasiness, though he had just given it as his reason for needing help. Ellicott hears the living speaker in it, in a way that precludes imitation.

Henry is warmest here. A good prayer prudently put in cannot be out of place in a discourse of divine things; a pious ejaculation does not break the coherence but adorns it. And he presses the size of the request: we are not straitened in the power and goodness of God, so why should we be straitened in our own faith and hope, which ought to be as large as the promise and need not be larger. He adds the observation that turns the thing on the hearers: under Pharaoh this increase was envied and complained of as a grievance, and under Moses it is rejoiced in and prayed for — which might have given them cause to remember with shame their talk of choosing a captain and going back to Egypt.

Clarke will not let the comparison with the stars pass as hyperbole, and works it out arithmetically. Abraham was told to look up with his naked eye, not through a glass, and only some three thousand stars can be seen that way from both hemispheres together, while the fighting men alone numbered above six hundred thousand at the census.

What Moses could not carry is defined precisely. Keil and Delitzsch take the burden and cumbrance to be the nation itself with all its affairs pressing on his shoulders; Ellicott notes that the word for cumbrance occurs in only one other place, where God says of Israel's feasts that he is weary to bear them; Wesley divides it into the labour of ruling a perverse people and the settling of their quarrels. Henry adds that Moses was not ambitious to monopolise the honour of government, though no man was ever better qualified for it.

The men to be found are described by three qualities, and Calvin takes them together. Wise means acute and perspicacious, not the crafty sense the word sometimes carries; understanding means sound judgment and discretion; and the third he reads actively, of men practised and tried, because none but the practised are competent for business. Neither the greatest probity nor diligence, he says, will do without skill and sagacity. Clarke glosses the same three as men who gained knowledge by labour, men of discernment, and men experienced in affairs. And Calvin fastens on who chooses them: they were not appointed by the will of Moses but elected by the votes of the people, and he calls that the most desirable kind of liberty — not to be compelled to obey whoever is tyrannically set over our heads, but that none should rule except he be approved by us. Moses waited for their consent, and attempted nothing that did not please them all.
16:
The charge to the judges is new matter. Gill notes that it is not recorded earlier, and Calvin explains why: the account in Exodus was concerned with how the change came about and gave the credit to Jethro, whereas here Moses omits his father-in-law and simply recalls to the people what he did with them.

The substance of it is impartiality, and the Hebrew idiom for the fault is physical. Both Wesley and Clarke render it as knowing or acknowledging faces, and both draw the same moral from it — sentence is to go by the merit of the cause and not by whether a man is rich or poor, friend or enemy. Wesley adds a curious parallel, that some of the Greek lawgivers required their judges to give sentence in the dark, where faces could not be seen. Clarke states the two ways of failing: neither the bold countenance of the mighty nor the abject look of the poor man is to move the bench, whether by favouring a poor man in a bad cause or by giving judgment against him at an oppressor's demand. Gill lists the distinctions that must not count — rich or poor, old or young, learned or unlearned — and concludes that truth and justice are to take place without regard to what persons are.

Calvin thinks the deeper danger is not contempt but fear. Judges often injure the poor out of contempt of them, but the commoner fault is the one Moses names: men otherwise just, and disposed to study what is equitable, swerve through fear of the threats of the powerful and dare not manfully face their ill will. What he demands is magnanimity — a willingness to bring the hatred of anyone upon oneself in defence of a good cause.

The reason given is the same in every hand, and it is the reason that carries the weight. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the phrase as meaning the judgment is appointed by God and to be administered in his name and according to his justice, which is why a case can be spoken of as brought before God. Calvin refuses to reduce it to a warning that an account must one day be rendered: the point is how absurd it is to leave the right course out of fear of a man, since by doing so the majesty of God, whose representatives they are, is prostituted and exposed to scorn. He sets Jehoshaphat's charge beside it — take heed what ye do, for ye judge not for man but for the Lord — and draws the encouragement out of the same fact, that a man doing God's work has God well able to keep him safe from the violence and the craftiness of the whole world. Clarke puts it in a line: ye minister in the place of God, act like him. Ellicott points forward instead, finding Paul's account of the magistrate an expansion of this one sentence.

Two smaller notes close the section. Wesley marks the inclusion of the stranger — one who deals or converses among them — and holds that justice was to be administered to such men equally with Israelites, partly for the honour of religion and partly because every man has an interest in matters of common right. And on the summary verse, Ellicott presses the phrase about that time: the commands given then were given on the road from Sinai to Kadesh-barnea, which he takes as confirming what he had argued about the opening verses of the chapter.
19:
The march itself gets one sentence and Henry gives it two purposes. Remembering the great and terrible wilderness should make them sensible of the goodness that guided and protected them through it — the memory of our dangers being what makes us thankful for deliverance — and it should also expose the folly of men who, in their discontent, proposed to go back through that same desert to Egypt, without any reason to expect they would be guided on so retrograde a march. Keil and Delitzsch identify the ground as the desert of et-Tih and note that the verb takes its object directly, of passing through a country.

Then they were at the border, and Henry marks how near. The land was set before them and they were told to go up and take it; he lets the reader see how close they stood to a happy settlement before they put a bar in their own door, which makes the sin appear the more exceedingly sinful. It will aggravate the ruin of hypocrites, he adds, that they were not far from the kingdom of God and still came short. Ellicott notices that the encouragement given here — fear not, neither be discouraged — reappears on the last night of Christ's life.

The spies are the crux, and the difficulty is a difference between two books. Henry lays the initiative squarely on the people: in Numbers it is said that the Lord directed the sending, but here we learn that the people asked for it first, and God in permitting it gave them up to their own counsels. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by the same route and adds the natural sequence — the proposal came from the people, Moses would refer it to the Lord, and once approved the scheme went forward. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the summons to go up is not expressly recorded in Numbers, but hold that it is implied there by the sending of the spies at all.

What the request actually amounted to is where Ellicott is sharpest. The people asked to be told by what way they should go up and into what cities they should come — but the Lord had gone before them all along precisely to search out places for them, so that here the guidance of the march is being taken into their own hands. He sets the contrast with Joshua's campaigns, in which no step was taken without divine direction, and concludes that the sending of the twelve, in the sense the people intended it, was an act of unbelief — as Moses himself will say a few verses later. Henry puts the same charge in his own idiom: Moses had given them God's word, and they could not find in their hearts to rely on it; human policy went further with them than divine wisdom, and they must needs light a candle to the sun. Gill's note softens nothing but adds a detail of temper — the proposal pleased Moses well, since he took it for a rational and prudent scheme and did not imagine it the effect of fear and distrust.

The report that came back is the last thing before the disaster, and it is unanimously good. Ellicott sets the wording here beside the fuller accounts, where the whole party grant that the land flows with milk and honey and Joshua and Caleb call it an exceeding good land; Gill lists what they carried down besides the famous cluster. Henry draws from that the observation the passage seems built for: the blessings God has promised are truly valuable and desirable, the unbelievers themselves being judges, since no one ever looked into that land but had to own it a good one.
26:
The murmuring is placed in the tents, and Gill takes that as where it started rather than where it stayed: they wept all night after the report, and then it became general and public and was brought against Moses and Aaron in a body. Calvin notes that the other account mentions the weeping too, and that Moses here keeps only the murmuring, which better suited his purpose in rebuking them.

What they said is the worst sentence in the chapter, and both Ellicott and Calvin say so. Ellicott calls it an astounding commentary on everything that had happened since Egypt, stronger than any complaint recorded in the older narrative. Calvin works out why it is so perverse: God could have given no more manifest proof of paternal love than that deliverance, and they repay it by complaining that they were brought out cruelly to die — construing his exceeding great love into hatred. He also revises his earlier impression of the spies: Moses had seemed to praise them for doing their work honestly, but the people's language shows they were the authors of the revolt, having by the terror they inspired made useless the very men they should have encouraged.

The report is quoted back in its own words. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the verb for discouraging as making the heart flow away, and defend the phrase about cities walled to heaven as no exaggeration but a rhetorical account of the impression actually received. Ellicott sets Caleb's later verdict beside it, that his brethren made the heart of the people melt; Wesley glosses the comparison as one of number, strength and valour. Clarke supplies a traveller's footnote on the walls: high walls are still reckoned defence enough against Arabs who will scarcely dismount to plunder, and the monastery on Sinai has no gate at all, only a basket let down on a pulley from an opening above.

Moses answered them, and the answer survives only here. Gill points out that the older narrative records nothing of what he said, only that he and Aaron fell on their faces; Keil and Delitzsch explain the omission by the outcome — the appeal failed, and the historical account keeps only the effort of Joshua and Caleb, because that had consequences for their own future. Calvin says the same in his own way, that Moses gives the heads of what he spoke and omits the address of the other two, and that all his pains were ineffectual.

The argument he used was from experience. Calvin has him setting the miracles they had already seen against the obstacles now in front of them, and notes the emphasis on before your eyes — the evidence of their own senses being what should have carried the conviction. Clarke observes that the Targum renders the promise as the Word of the Lord shall fight for you, a term the Chaldee paraphrases use exactly as John uses his. Ellicott points out the irony that finished the appeal: the reminder that God went before them could not avail with people who had already chosen men to go before them.

The image at the end is the one everyone stops over. Calvin says the way would simply not have been passable unless God had borne them as a father carries an infant, which exalts his condescension and at the same time reminds them of their own weakness — elsewhere Moses keeps part of the same figure and compares him to an eagle bearing her young. Ellicott traces Paul's phrase about God bearing them in the wilderness to this verse. And Keil and Delitzsch mark what follows it grammatically: the participle for their not believing describes unbelief not as a lapse but as a settled condition, which is what makes it so grievous in men whose guide and defence went visibly before them the whole way.
34:
Calvin begins with the word for God's hearing. Nothing can be concealed from him, and he will take account of every word and deed — men would never dare to murmur if they did not promise themselves impunity on the pretext that he pays no attention to what is done here below. From the same clause Calvin draws the opposite comfort: a just judge does not proceed hastily, and shows no severity without a full examination of the case. Clarke states the verdict plainly: his justice was incensed, and he could not have been a just God if it had not been.

The sentence is an oath, and Ellicott hears it echoed twice afterwards — in the psalm where God swears in his wrath that they should not enter into his rest, and in the parable where none of the men that were bidden shall taste the supper. Calvin puts the loss sharply: they deprived themselves of an assured inheritance at the moment they were about to receive it.

Two exceptions are named separately. Ellicott observes the arrangement — Caleb stands by himself as the exception among the people, Joshua apart as the exception among the leaders. Wesley reads Caleb as including Joshua by implication, since Joshua was no longer one of the people but set over them; Gill notes that the condemnation covered not only the ten who brought the report but the whole body that credited it.

Moses' own exclusion is inserted out of its chronological place, and Ellicott explains why it belongs. It was an event of the fortieth year, folded in with the rejection of the people in the second, because the reason in both cases was unbelief. As the spies presumed to settle the route and order of the conquest, a matter of divine guidance, so Moses presumed to alter the prescribed order of a miracle; like transgressions incurred like penalties, and the fault the people suffered for could not be overlooked in their leader. Calvin defends the phrase for your sakes against the charge of evasion. Moses is not extenuating his guilt before God — that would only double the evil — but reproving the people justly, since the occasion of his fall arose from them, and they were so perverse that even he was drawn into their guilt and its punishment. Wesley says as much in a line: their perverseness provoked him to speak unadvisedly.

Joshua's appointment is set beside the sentence deliberately. Calvin calls it a notable ground of hope, that the people should hear provision already made against the day Moses would be gone; why this man was preferred, especially when Caleb is more highly praised elsewhere, he leaves with God, who chooses according to his own will so that a man's dignity depends on gratuitous favour. He also notices the sting in the description: to stand before a man is to be at his bidding, so the order is inverted when a servant is made his master's successor. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the phrase the same way and take the charge to strengthen him as pointing to his formal installation.

Then the children, and Calvin makes the limit of the pardon do a great deal of work. God tempers the judgment so that none of the guilty escapes while the covenant with Abraham stands inviolate, and shows mercy on the very children their parents had given up for a prey. That the grace is confined to those too young to discern good from evil shows that everyone past the years of reason was an accomplice, the contagion having spread through the whole body. And he blocks an inference some have drawn, that infants are therefore free of original sin: the passage distinguishes children from those who consciously provoked God, and says nothing of the root of corruption, which is not absent merely because it has not yet borne fruit.
41:
The repentance arrives, and no witness will call it that. Ellicott sets the emphatic we of this verse beside the we of the earlier complaint and finds the same thing in both — a we without God — and calls the movement a change from cowardice to presumption, not from unbelief to faith. Calvin says it came too late and was never serious: when they ought to have borne God's chastening patiently they tried to shake it off by a new act of disobedience, and did nothing but kick against the pricks. What most struck him is the sequence. They now attempt against God's will, and with his help expressly withdrawn, the very thing they had refused to attempt under his command and with a sure promise of success — and hypocrisy so blinds men that they imagined they were making up for the evil they were in fact doubling. Gill supplies the ordinary motive underneath: they had no wish to go back into the wilderness by the way of the Red Sea, whatever they had said earlier about returning to Egypt.

The prohibition is absolute and comes in two parts. Calvin marks that God does not merely forbid the battle but denies them his assistance, which is the whole difference between this attack and the one they would not make. Gill dates the word to the moment they were armed and moving.

The defeat is described by a simile, and it is the simile the witnesses stop over. Clarke reads it as irresistible numbers; Wesley draws out the behaviour — bees provoked come out of the hive in a body and pursue their disturber with fury. Ellicott takes the mention as evidence about the writer: the detail is incidental, and shows a man familiar with the sight of a company of men chased by bees, which is worth noting beside what is said elsewhere about the hornet. On the place he is more cautious, taking the Seir here for the hills about Petra rather than the Seir in Judah, and reporting that Hormah's site is unknown and that a Jewish commentator was not sure whether the word is a place-name at all or simply means utter destruction. Gill notes that the Amorites had help, the Amalekites joining in the attack.

They came back and wept, and Ellicott points out that this is not in the older account at all — a fact which shows the personal knowledge of the writer and that the narrative is not simply drawn from the earlier books. Gill fills in the scene at the door of the tabernacle and what the tears were for: the slaughter, the sin, the sentence of return, and very probably a prayer that they might not be turned back after all. Calvin treats the weeping as evidence they themselves supplied. Nothing but the force of their own feelings would have brought them to it, so that they were abundantly convinced the punishment was just — and having convicted themselves, they had no ground to complain that God proved implacable.

The last verse gives a duration that nobody can fix. Calvin reports the readings — that they stayed another forty days, or that the phrase is simply an indefinite expression for a long time — and prefers the second, drawing from it a picture of a people lying stupefied for want of knowing what to do. He adds one identification for the sake of clarity: the Kadesh meant is Kadesh-barnea, from which the spies were sent, and not the Kadesh where Miriam died and the people murmured for water.
